## Introduction: approximation in a finite dimensional subspace

Work with real-valued functions in $H=L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mu)$, with

$$
\langle u,v\rangle=\int uv\,d\mu,
\qquad
\|u\|_2^2=\langle u,u\rangle.
$$

Let $L_k\subset H$ have an orthogonal basis $\{b_1,\ldots,b_k\}$. Write $b(x)=(b_1(x),\ldots,b_k(x))^\top$, so every $h\in L_k$ has a unique representation $h=\beta^\top b$.

For $g\in H$, its orthogonal projection onto $L_k$ is

$$
\Pi g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h\in L_k}\|g-h\|_2^2.
$$

Because $L_k$ is finite-dimensional, it is closed. The Hilbert-space projection theorem therefore guarantees a unique minimizer.[^projection] The goal is to compute it from the basis functions.

## Statement: the projection coefficients are explicit

For every $g\in H$,

$$
(\Pi g)(x)
=\sum_{i=1}^k
\frac{\langle g,b_i\rangle}{\|b_i\|_2^2}\,b_i(x).
\tag{1}
$$

This equality is understood $\mu$-almost everywhere. Orthogonality does not require unit norms: the denominators disappear only when the basis is **orthonormal**.

## Motivation: a function approximation becomes least squares

A choice of $k$ basis functions reduces approximation in $L^2$ to optimization over $k$ real coefficients. Orthogonality makes the quadratic term diagonal, so each coefficient can be solved separately. This is the same geometry that underlies ordinary least squares.

## Derivation

### 1. Expand the objective in basis coordinates

Define

$$
\Omega=\operatorname{diag}
\bigl(\|b_1\|_2^2,\ldots,\|b_k\|_2^2\bigr),
\qquad
c=\int b(x)g(x)\,d\mu(x).
$$

Since $\langle b_i,b_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
J(\beta)
&=\int\{g(x)-\beta^\top b(x)\}^2\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\|g\|_2^2
-2\sum_{i=1}^k\beta_i\langle g,b_i\rangle
+\sum_{i=1}^k\beta_i^2\|b_i\|_2^2\\
&=\|g\|_2^2-2\beta^\top c+\beta^\top\Omega\beta.
\end{aligned}
$$

### 2. Find the unique minimizer

Differentiating with respect to the coefficient vector gives

$$
\nabla J(\beta)=2(\Omega\beta-c),
\qquad
\nabla^2J(\beta)=2\Omega.
$$

Every basis function is nonzero, so $\Omega$ is positive definite. Thus $J$ is **strongly convex**, and solving $\nabla J(\beta)=0$ gives

$$
\widehat\beta=\Omega^{-1}c,
\qquad
\widehat\beta_i
=\frac{\langle g,b_i\rangle}{\|b_i\|_2^2}
\tag{2}
$$

Completing the square also proves uniqueness directly:

$$
J(\beta)-J(\widehat\beta)
=(\beta-\widehat\beta)^\top
\Omega(\beta-\widehat\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^k\|b_i\|_2^2
(\beta_i-\widehat\beta_i)^2.
$$

This difference is strictly positive whenever $\beta\ne\widehat\beta$. Substituting (2) into $\Pi g=\widehat\beta^\top b$ proves (1).

The residual is orthogonal to every basis function:

$$
\langle g-\Pi g,b_i\rangle
=\langle g,b_i\rangle-\widehat\beta_i\|b_i\|_2^2
=0.
$$

Consequently, adding and subtracting $\Pi g$ gives, for any $h\in L_k$,

$$
\|g-h\|_2^2
=\|(g-\Pi g)+(\Pi g-h)\|_2^2
=\|g-\Pi g\|_2^2+\|\Pi g-h\|_2^2.
$$

The cross term vanishes because $\Pi g-h\in L_k$.

### 3. Write the projection as an operator

Define the synthesis operator and its adjoint by

$$
B:\mathbb{R}^k\to H,
\qquad B\beta=\beta^\top b,
\qquad
B^*g=
\begin{pmatrix}
\langle g,b_1\rangle\\
\vdots\\
\langle g,b_k\rangle
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Orthogonality gives $B^*B=\Omega$. Since $c=B^*g$, equation (2) becomes

$$
\Pi=B\Omega^{-1}B^*
\tag{3}
$$

Here $B^*$ takes inner products with the basis functions. With $b(x)$ written as a column vector, the explicit formula is

$$
(\Pi g)(x)
=b(x)^\top\Omega^{-1}
\int b(y)g(y)\,d\mu(y).
$$

The integral is the operation represented by the adjoint; it cannot be replaced by pointwise multiplication.

### 4. Relate the calculation to Fourier coefficients

You can derive the same conclusion using orthonormal basis $\{\theta_j\}_{j\geq 1}$ of $L_2(\mathcal{X})$. If $H$ has a complete orthonormal basis $\{\theta_j\}_{j\ge1}$, define

$$
\widehat g_j=\langle g,\theta_j\rangle,
\qquad
\widehat b_{ij}=\langle b_i,\theta_j\rangle.
$$

and

$$
r_\beta = g - \sum^k_{i=1} \beta_i b_i
$$

Then, Parseval's identity gives the equivalent objective[^parseval]

$$
J(\beta) = \|r_\beta\|^2_2 \stackrel{*}{=} \sum^\infty_{j=1}|\langle r_\beta, \theta_j\rangle|^2
=\sum_{j=1}^\infty
\left(\widehat g_j-\sum_{i=1}^k
\beta_i\widehat b_{ij}\right)^2.
$$

The minimizer of the RHS of the equality induces the same $\hat\beta_i$. The sequence $\widehat g=(\widehat g_j)_{j\ge1}$ consists of generalized Fourier coefficients; it is not a function to add to $g$. This change of coordinates is optional.

## A quick check

Take $d=1$, $d\mu(x)=\mathbf{1}_{[-1,1]}(x)\,dx$, and $L_2=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\}$. These two basis functions are orthogonal but not normalized. For $g(x)=x^2+x$,

$$
\Omega=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0\\
0&2/3
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
c=
\begin{pmatrix}
2/3\\
2/3
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\widehat\beta=
\begin{pmatrix}
1/3\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Hence $(\Pi g)(x)=x+1/3$. The residual $x^2-1/3$ is orthogonal to both basis functions:

$$
\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1/3)\,dx=0,
\qquad
\int_{-1}^1x(x^2-1/3)\,dx=0.
$$

[^projection]: Axler, S. (2020). *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis*. Springer. Section 8B, results 8.28 and 8.37, establish existence, uniqueness, and the orthogonality characterization. [Open-access text](https://measure.axler.net/MIRA.pdf#page=241).

[^parseval]: Axler, *Measure, Integration & Real Analysis*, Section 8C, result 8.63 (Parseval's identity). [Open-access text](https://measure.axler.net/MIRA.pdf#page=259).
